items.title: Delhi’s chest clinics are filling up as toxic air takes its toll
items.summary: In August 2026, the health ministry issued a notice directing all district hospitals and medical colleges to set up chest clinics, to be operational between September and February. The National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) then issued guidelines for these clinics. They are to be staffed with the medical personnel needed to examine and treat patients, who are also to be counselled on how to avoid pollution-related illnesses and what precautions to take. On November 6, the Delhi health department directed district hospitals to open these clinics within a week. Newslaundry visited hospitals in Burari, Jahangirpuri, and GTB Nagar – areas badly affected by pollution. In Burari and Jahangirpuri, road dust is a major contributor; and it is hard to even stand on the street without a mask. In Burari, we met Geeta, a local resident, who has had a cough, chest pain and breathing difficulties since Diwali. Watch our report. items.title: Why the Siang dam protests matter beyond Arunachal
items.summary: Inevitably, when one story dominates the news cycle, many other developing stories get buried or even forgotten. This column is to remind you of one such story, a story that began in 1982 in Arunachal Pradesh, a state about which we know precious little, barring the fact that it borders China. Those of us who live in the ‘mainland’ became aware of unrest in this border state recently when locals came out in numbers to protest a large dam project on the Siang river. In one instance, in the town of Pasighat , on the banks of the Siang, the protest turned violent; arrests were made, and people supporting the protests were intimidated. Why should protests against a dam in Arunachal Pradesh interest people in the rest of the country? Because these protests are not just about one dam. They remind us, yet again, that successive governments continue to push policies where people, mostly from indigenous communities, and the environment are considered the necessary “collateral damage” in the larger national interest. items.title: PMLA Adjudicating Authority cannot confirm ED's property attachment without judicial member: Supreme Court
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that the adjudicating authority confirming the provisional attachment of properties by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) must include a judicial member. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana also ruled that the attachment cannot be confirmed by a single-member adjudicating authority unless that member is a judicial member. The Bench observed that the adjudication carries substantial consequences for the civil and consequential constitutional rights of the person whose property has been attached by the ED. "If the Adjudicating Authority finds that the property is involved in money laundering, the provisions of Sections 8(3) and 8(4) are attracted and possession of the property is taken over by the Government of India. Such dispossession may well endure until the conclusion of the trial for the offence of money laundering, depriving the person of the use of the property for a considerable period before the offence is proved," the Court said. items.title: Tryst with the Constitution: Parliament must debate
items.summary: In his final address to the Constituent Assembly, Dr BR Ambedkar famously remarked that the success of a Constitution depends, in large measure, on the people who are called upon to work it. If they happen to be a ‘good lot’, even a bad Constitution may turn out to be good. The functioning of the Constituent Assembly, the intellectual rigour of its deliberations and, more importantly, the attitude of its members proved that they were indeed such ‘good people’. 77 years later, as we celebrate Constitution Day, we must revisit the spirit of deliberation that characterised the making of our Constitution. Deliberation, dissent, consensus A remarkable feature of the Indian Constitution is the extent to which it was discussed and debated before it took its final shape. Prior to the appointment of the Drafting Committee, the Assembly constituted numerous committees to examine specific aspects of the Constitution and make recommendations. These recommendations, as approved by the Assembly, formed the basis of the initial draft prepared by Sir BN Rau, which was subsequently scrutinised and revised by the Drafting Committee led by Dr Ambedkar. A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana took note of the rising number of complaints and applications filed before the adjudicating authority. It added that the increasing caseload, coupled with the time-bound nature of adjudication, puts enormous pressure on the members of the adjudicating authority. The Bench noted that before the 2009 amendment, the PMLA provided for setting up more than one adjudicating authority. It said the Centre could consider restoring that original framework.
